newsitem.title: USA: Simpson jury urged to impose stiff punitive damages.
newsitem.headline: Simpson jury urged to impose stiff punitive damages.

text.p: The plaintiffs in O.J. Simpson's civil trial on Thursday urged jurors to punish him by imposing heavy damages for the deaths of his ex-wife and her friend on top of $8.5 million they already awarded.

Daniel Petrocelli, the plaintiffs' lead attorney, said Simpson violated the rights of the victims in taking their lives, adding, "We are not just talking about any violations, we are talking about the most unconscionable violations."
The jury on Tuesday blamed Simpson for the June 12, 1994, murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman and ordered him to pay $8.5 million in compensatory damages.
Simpson, acquitted on criminal murder charges in 1995, was absent from the courtroom on Thursday as the four-month trial entered its final phase.

Attorney John Kelly, representing the estate of Nicole Brown Simpson, told the panel that by imposing substantial punitive damages it could ensure that "no man, especially a man of fame and fortune, will ever again act with such reckless disregard for human life as Mr. Simpson did."

But Simpson's attorney, Robert Baker, argued Simpson had been punished enough and urged jurors to award "zero punitive damages," saying to do otherwise would amount to "piling on and attempting to destroy Mr. Simpson."
Baker said Simpson had no assets and owed lawyers and mortgage payments. "He has no equity in his home, he has no savings," he added.
In assessing punitive damages jurors will be instructed by the judge to base their decision on how reprehensible the crime was and how much the award would hurt Simpson financially.

The $8.5 million award for the death of Goldman, which will go to his divorced parents, is the largest in recent years for a male victim aged 25 to 29, according to a group of legal researchers called Jury Verdict Research. Goldman was 25 when he died.
Any punitive damages would be shared by Goldman's family and the estate of Nicole Brown Simpson, whose heirs are her two young children.

Jurors, who were expected to begin their second round of deliberations on Friday, were presented Thursday with an array of conflicting figures about Simpson's wealth or lack of it. His financial statements indicated that at the end of last year he had a negative net worth of more than $800,000, meaning his debts were greater than his assets.

Baker told the jurors that taking into account Tuesday's $8.5 million judgment against him, Simpson had a negative net worth of more than $9 million. In addition he said Simpson could no longer make money by selling his name and signing autographs.

But Neill Freeman, an accountant and financial investigator testifying for the plaintiffs, strongly disagreed with Simpson's estimate of his worth and his future earning powers. Freeman accused Simpson of overstating his liabilities and understating his assets in "incomplete" financial information.

Far from being broke, Freeman said, Simpson had a net worth of more than $15.7 million as of Dec. 31, 1996. In addition, he said he had calculated Simpson's future earning potential for the rest of his life at about $24.9 million from selling his "name and likeness" in the form of product endorsements and autograph signing at home and abroad.

Freeman said he determined in 1996 Simpson received $1.75 million from his insurance company for legal costs and a further $1.25 million from a food processing company he had investments in for a total of $3 million.
But during that period Freeman said he could find no evidence that Simpson had paid off any debts. "I don't understand where the cash went," he said.
Mark Roesler, a sports memorabilia agent, said he estimated Simpson's potential earnings at between $2 million and $3 million a year for the rest of his life.
He said Simpson, since his acquittal on murder charges, had applied for six trademarks covering 500 items, including photos, toys, sporting goods, jewelry and clothing.
The trademarks were for the names, "Team O.J. Justice for All," "The Juice," "O.J. Simpson" with his picture, "O.J. Simpson" without a picture, "Juice" and "O.J."
Meanwhile a CNN/USA Today poll published Thursday found that the jury's finding in Simpson's civil case had split the country along racial lines, as did the verdict in his criminal trial.
The poll found that most whites agreed with the civil court jury while the majority of blacks disagreed -- just the opposite of the racial division of opinion over Simpson's criminal acquittal.
